title: Fast merging of summaries for symmetric streaming computations
formal: Does every total, order-invariant Boolean stream function computable deterministically in polylogarithmic space and polylogarithmic time per item also admit a deterministic summary scheme with polylogarithmic message size, working space, and time per merge, correct for every binary merge tree? The uniform families, input lengths and costs in this question are specified below.
why: Fast merging would allow any efficiently maintained order-independent statistic to be computed from independently processed pieces without an expensive reconstruction step. A separation would expose an inherent computational cost of parallel aggregation even when communication and memory are small.
status_note: The cited paper establishes a space-preserving simulation but explicitly identifies its high running time as a limitation. This card selects a precise uniform polylogarithmic-time refinement, with no promise or randomness. No matching general simulation or separation was located in the bounded September 2026 check; the literal malformed source sentence is not treated as evidence.

sentences: The input statistic is a total Boolean function invariant under reordering the stream.
A streaming program computes it using polylogarithmic memory and time per item.
The selected question asks for equally efficient local summaries and merging on every binary aggregation tree.
A known simulation preserves small space but can use superpolynomial merge time.
The target excludes promise and randomness separations and does not require identical intermediate summaries.

definitions: For each integer \(N\geq2\), let \(f_N\) map every nonempty sequence over \([N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\) of length at most \(N\) to one bit. Totality means every such sequence is in its domain. Order invariance means permuting any sequence leaves its value unchanged; it is stronger than merely swapping two players. A streaming algorithm is one fixed deterministic program given \(N\) in binary, which starts with an initialized state, reads one item at a time, and produces \(f_N(x)\) when the stream ends. There must be constants \(B,c\), depending on the family but not \(N\), for which initialization, each update and final output take at most \(B\log^c(N+2)\) steps, and the stored state and temporary workspace use that many bits. A merge scheme consists of three fixed deterministic programs: a map \(\Phi_N\) from one item to a summary, a map \(\mu_N\) from two summaries to a summary, and a decoder \(\eta_N\) from a summary to a bit. Summaries may include their represented length. For every valid sequence and every rooted binary tree whose leaves are its items in any order, apply \(\Phi_N\) at the leaves, \(\mu_N\) at internal nodes and \(\eta_N\) at the root. The resulting bit must equal \(f_N(x)\). Intermediate summaries may depend on the tree; only the decoded answer must be invariant. Each message, workspace and invocation time is bounded by \(B_1\log^{c_1}(N+2)\), for constants depending on the family. Time means steps of a standard deterministic multitape Turing machine on binary representations; input and output tapes have the usual sequential access. The programs receive \(N\) and their local arguments, with no advice or precomputed data depending on \(N\). Both models are exact and deterministic. The conclusion is existence of a merge scheme for each streaming-computable family, not a promised efficient compiler from arbitrary program descriptions.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal simulation, including the time, memory and arbitrary-tree guarantees. Alternatively give a total symmetric family with a qualifying streaming algorithm and prove that no qualifying merge scheme exists. A slow merge procedure with short messages, a separation using a promise, or a private-randomness separation does not decide this specified question.

context_blocks.text: The workshop page asks broadly whether good streaming algorithms yield good sketches and compares one-way with simultaneous communication. Editorial specialization: this card selects the deterministic, total-function question with efficient merging. This is the time-sensitive refinement motivated by the paper cited on that page, rather than a claim that the already established space-only simulation remains unknown.

Feldman, Muthukrishnan, Sidiropoulos, Stein and Svitkina show that symmetric deterministic streaming computation can be distributed through a binary aggregation tree with comparable message size and polynomially related space. Their simulation uses reachability search and can take superpolynomial time. The retained target asks whether that time cost can always be avoided.

A sequential chain of merges is itself a streaming computation. The converse must support balanced trees and every other arrangement, even when the stream algorithm’s intermediate states record order-dependent information that disappears from the final answer.

The cited paper also gives failures of analogous comparisons for promises, multiple permissible outputs and private randomness. This card removes those routes to a separation by requiring a total Boolean function and deterministic exact computation. The malformed final sentence on the workshop page is not used as a theorem statement.

Associativity of the summary representation is not required: two different trees can leave different internal summaries provided both decode correctly. Demanding identical summaries would strengthen the problem beyond the aggregation model used here.

Recent turnstile-to-linear-sketch simulations address algebraic update streams and space preservation. Their hypotheses and conclusions do not provide this uniform polylogarithmic-time merging theorem for arbitrary insertion streams and arbitrary total symmetric functions.
